newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Smooth Philippine water bids seen reassuring investors.
newsitem.headline: Smooth Philippine water bids seen reassuring investors.

text.p: The smooth privatisation of Manila's water system should reassure foreign investors made jittery by recent problems with other high-profile projects in the Philippines, officials and analysts said.

Although the threat of litigation still hangs over the privatisation of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), the bidding for contracts to take over operations was well handled by the government, they said on Saturday.
Ensuring the bidding process was objective and transparent was a top priority, said an official with World Bank-affiliate International Finance Corp (IFC), the adviser to the privatisation programme.
"We believe we have succeeded in that objective. We believe that all the bidders will concur with that judgement," said Scott Macleod, manager of Corporate Finance Services for IFC.
The smooth handling of the water privatisation should help offset criticism of other recent privatisation projects and encourage more foreign investment, he said
Earlier this year, the government cancelled the bidding for privatising a container terminal at the Subic Bay economic zone and ordered it held anew.
The sale of the historic Manila Hotel, a project to develop reclaimed land in Manila Bay and the construction of a 1,200 mw power plant have also run into problems.
The MWSS contracts were considered one of the largest water privatisation projects in the world.
The two winning consortia are expected to invest $7.0 billion over the 25-year term of the contracts to improve an outmoded system and bring water to 98 percent of the capital's 11 million people.

Some of the world's biggest utility companies put in bids in collaboration with local business groups. The two contracts were awarded to a consortium of local conglomerate Ayala Corp, Bechtel Corp of the United States and Britain's United Utilities and to the combine of Benpres Holdings Corp and France's Lyonnaise des Eaux
The bidding process was almost held back when newspapers reported two weeks ago that the Ayala-Bechtel-United group had submitted a technically-flawed bid.
Ayala and the MWSS had denied the reports.
Christopher Glynn, chief commercial officer of the British Embassy in Manila, said the speculation of flawed bids during the technical review was expected.
"It happens anywhere in the world," he said. "Its fair as it could possibly be. By and large the people running the whole thing tried their best."

"People always reserve themselves a right to review. Whatever they decide, they always still see a lot of investment opportunities," said Guillermo Luz, executive director of Makati Business Club, which groups the top corporations in the country.

He pointed out the Philippines is committed to privatisation in order to build up its infrastructure. Foreign investors will see opportunities in other water districts in the country, and in port and transportation development, he said.

The bidding process had also been threatened by litigation as officials of Rizal province near Manila and MWSS workers tried to stop the privatisation. A Manila regional trial court said it would issue a decision soon.
"We do believe that there is not much ground for that complaint and we are helpful it will be settled speedily," said Martin Negre, the Asia-Pacific president of Lyonnaise des Eaux.
